title: Errors in a design critique tool
excerpt: If a comment fails, keep the sentence on screen and say whether it was saved, and on which version. A vanished pin with a vanished toast loses the critique.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band, looking for a note that should still be on the frame.
caption: Both of them need to see whether the note survived. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should happen when a comment fails to save?
faqs.answer: Keep the text and the pin, and say it was not saved, without clearing the composer. If you are unsure, keep the draft until you know. A mention or a notification can fail without deleting the note, so say which part failed.

faqs.question: What if a new version lands while someone is commenting?
faqs.answer: Save the note on the draft they were looking at, say so, and let them copy it forward if the point still stands. Do not silently move the pin onto pixels that changed. An upload that fails should leave reviewers on the last good frame.

faqs.question: How is a permission limit different from a crash?
faqs.answer: A person who can view but not comment should read that sentence, not 'this file failed to load.' Resolve can fail while a reply is kept, and the note should stay open until resolve actually succeeds. False resolution changes the product.

markdown:
Honest design critique tool error states tell a small team what broke, whether their comment was saved, and how to put it on the right screen. A code and a sad illustration waste the thought they just had about the work.

The W3C's WCAG overview groups the guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A failed comment has to be readable as text and understandable as a next step. A pin that vanishes, with a toast that vanishes faster, fails both.

## Did the note survive

The reviewer's sentence is the work product. The screen has to say one of three things.

- The comment is on the frame, saved.
- The comment is not saved, and the text is still in the composer.
- You are not sure, and the text is still in the composer until you are.

Clearing the composer on a failed request is the defect to design out. People will not retype a careful critique, especially if they are in a meeting and the moment has moved on. Keep the words. Keep the pin location. Offer to try again. If the retry might duplicate the note, say that you will update the same one rather than add a second.

Show the failure on the note itself, or in the composer, not in a corner toast. Critique happens while someone is looking at pixels. A peripheral message will be missed, and the team will argue later about a comment that never landed. The words "Not saved" on the draft are enough. Color can support them. Color cannot be the only signal.

If the save succeeded and the notification failed, say that too. "Your comment is on the frame. Sam was not notified. You can mention them again." Those are different recoveries. A single "error" teaches the team to assume the worst and to paste the same note into chat, which splits the record.

## Version, pin, and the frame that moved

A comment can fail because it is attached to a version that just got replaced. Say which version they were on, and where the text went. "This draft was updated while you were writing. Your note is saved on Thursday's draft, not on the new one." Give them a way to copy it onto the new frame if the point still stands. Do not silently re-pin it. The pixels moved. A pin in the old corner may now accuse the wrong headline.

A pin that lands off the frame, because the layout shifted or the coordinates were nonsense, should be kept with the comment and flagged. "This note is not attached to a point. Open it from the list." The list becomes the recovery. Deleting the note because the geometry failed is punishing the writer for your math.

Upload failures are the designer's error, not the reviewer's. "The new version did not upload. Reviewers are still on Thursday's draft." Leave the old frame in place. Do not swap in a broken image and let new comments attach to a gray box. If the file is too large or the wrong type, say the limit in the same sentence as the failure, and keep them on the version that works.

A live URL that will not capture should fall back in words. "We could not freeze this page. Comments would drift. Try a still export, or retry the capture." Letting people pin a page you could not freeze creates notes that move overnight. Refuse the pin, explain the refusal, and keep any text they already typed.

## Mentions, resolve, and the second person

Mentioning a teammate can fail when they are not on the review, or when their seat was removed. "Sam is not on this file. The comment is saved. Add Sam if they should see it." Do not drop the comment because the mention failed. The sentence about the design still matters. The notification is secondary.

Resolving can fail. "This note is still open. Your reply is saved." Or, if the reply also failed, "Still open, and your reply is only on this device until you retry." Be precise. A note that looks resolved on one screen and open on another is how a team ships the thing someone asked to change. When you are unsure, prefer showing it open. An unresolved note is annoying. A falsely resolved one changes the product.

Two people editing the same note, or resolving while the author edits, need a human sentence. "Riley resolved this while you were editing. Your new text is kept below. Put it back on the note if you still want it." Keep both texts. A merge dialog full of technical conflict markers is the wrong voice for a critique. This is a small team, not a source-control seminar.

## The file and the list can fail apart

If the comment list loads and the image does not, show the list and say the frame failed. People can still read the critique. If the image loads and the list does not, show the frame and say the notes failed to load, with a retry that does not discard a draft in progress. A full-screen error for a partial failure throws away the half that worked.

A missing permission should not look like a missing file. "You can view this review. You cannot comment." That is a limit, and it belongs in the permissions conversation. "This file failed to load" is a different sentence, used only when the file actually failed. Mixing them sends the team hunting for a broken upload when the real issue is a seat.

Search and filters create false errors here too. "No unresolved notes" is a success if everything is resolved. "Could not load notes" is a failure. "Filtered to mentions of you, and there are none" is a filter. Three sentences. One empty illustration cannot say all three, so do not depend on the illustration.

## Write the lines before the icons

List the failures that can happen and write the line a designer would say across a table.

- The comment was not saved, and the text is still here.
- It saved on the previous version, not the new one.
- The frame did not upload, and reviewers are still on the last good draft.
- The mention failed, and the comment remains.
- Resolve failed, and the note is still open.
- You can view and not comment, which is a limit, not a crash.

Try the lines in a meeting, with the frame on a shared screen. The sentence has to be readable by the person not holding the mouse. If "not saved" is a whisper in a side panel, the room will keep talking and the note will die. Put the status where the note is. After the meeting, open the same file on another person's seat and confirm the note is either there for both of you or still marked unsent for the author. A note that exists for one and not the other, with no status, is the bug this screen is for.

Read them against a real file. If a line does not say whether the sentence survived, rewrite it. If an icon is clearer than the line, the line is weak. Fix the line. The icon can stay as support. A crumpled-paper drawing with the real news in small type under it is how the news gets missed in a meeting.

Attachments on a comment fail often enough to deserve their own line. "The note is saved. The image did not upload. Retry the image, or leave the note without it." Do not roll back the sentence because the file was large. The sentence is the critique. The image is evidence. Keep the one you have, and name the one you lost. If the image arrives on the second try, attach it to the same note so the thread does not split in two.

Also decide the offline case, because reviews happen on trains. If they can comment offline, the note should say "Saved on this device. Not on the file yet." When the connection returns, it should say it landed, or that it did not. A spinner that ends with no sentence is not a sync strategy.

## The limit that looks like a bug

View-only guests, clients, and teammates who can comment but not resolve will tap things the role forbids. Those taps need a reason, not a failure code. [Permissions in a design critique tool](/blog/permissions-in-a-design-critique-tool) is the next piece. It covers how to show what a small team can do, and why a control is absent, so nobody files a bug for a boundary you intended.

Hanabi treats the unsent note as a first-class state in Figma and in the build. Next.js, React, and TypeScript can keep the draft beside the frame. The version, the pin, and the save state belong in PostgreSQL through Prisma, so a retry knows which note it is continuing. Tailwind can make "not saved" obvious without turning the review into an alarm. Motion should confirm a real save, not decorate a failure.

If your team retypes critique into chat because the tool drops it, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the last note that disappeared. The sentence on the screen should have been shorter than the apology.
